name: The Witch Tree of Black Kate

location.address: Landgoed Ten Vorsel, 5531 ND Bladel, North Brabant, Netherlands
location.neighbourhood: Ten Vorsel estate, Bladel (roughly 16 km from Hilvarenbeek)

access: Free, in the Ten Vorsel forest estate near Bladel, on the region's own listed walking routes (visitbladel.nl lists it under hiking destinations, with a plotted route to it). A low sheep-fence was placed around the trunk from mid-2019 to stop root-plate erosion from the volume of visitors it now draws; visitors can still walk right up to it, just not trample the roots.
transport: No direct public transport to the estate. About 16 km / 20-25 minutes by car from central Hilvarenbeek; a day-trip stop rather than part of the same walk as the Gebodenlinde (hvb_001).
verify_notes: 2020 European Tree of the Year, rank 4, 18,452 votes. Won the Dutch national 'Boom van het Jaar' (Tree of the Year) contest first, in 2019, organised by SBNL Natuurfonds, chosen from 148 nominated trees narrowed to 12 (one per province); that win made it the Dutch entry in the European final. IMPORTANT HONESTY NOTE FOR THE WRITER: at about 130 years old this is a young tree by this project's usual bar, and its own species is explicitly unremarkable -- Jan Rots of Bosgroep Zuid-Nederland, the forestry group involved with the estate, is quoted on record (Omroep Brabant, 2019) saying so directly: 'De soort, een beuk, is niet bijzonder' (the species, a beech, is nothing special), and even 'het verhaal van Zwarte Kaat is uit de dikke duim gezogen' (the Zwarte Kaat legend is made up / fabricated). What clears the bar here is NOT age: it is the tree's genuinely strange growth form (spectacle visible in a photograph) plus a documented legend (a story with a named literary source), and the page should lean on those two, never on age. Species: European Beech, Fagus sylvatica, confirmed by all sources including the Dutch Wikipedia article, which cites the tree's own entry in the Landelijk Register van Monumentale Bomen (the Bomenstichting's national monumental-tree register, tree number 1678572) -- an official register entry independent of both the contest and the newspaper coverage, and itself a second source on top of Wikipedia and Omroep Brabant. MEASUREMENTS (Dutch Wikipedia, citing the register and a 2019/2021 remeasurement): trunk circumference 3.21 m measured 3 March 2021; height 17.90 m measured 6 December 2019 by triangulation; crown diameter 20.60 m. Age is estimated (not exactly documented) from its form, crown growth and trunk girth cross-checked against old estate maps, and the register/Wikipedia date it to 'around 1890'. THE SHAPE: unusually short trunk with a wildly irregular, gnarled crown, and roots that sit partly ABOVE the ground surface rather than growing down into it, caused by hard-to-penetrate clay layers in the subsoil plus erosion from foot traffic -- this is the visual spectacle the legend was hung on. THE LEGEND, to be told clearly as legend: named for 'Zwarte Kaat' ('Black Kate'), the supposed leader of a gang of highway robbers and smugglers who, according to a story first published by the Bladel-born writer Renier Snieders in 1852 ('Het Kind met den Helm'), stole the local lord of Ten Vorsel's child, was caught years later and beheaded; refused burial in consecrated ground or a grave marked with a cross, she was reputedly buried on the heath under a shrub and a young beech instead, which grew into this tree. The estate's own manager (Rob Raijmakers, Landgoed Ten Vorsel, quoted alongside Jan Rots) says the tree 'speaks to the imagination', standing alone in open ground with roots that look like they never managed to grow into the earth, and that passers-by at dusk have been startled by it. The beech originally stood alone on open heathland; when the Maatschappij van Welstand and the Heidemaatschappij reclaimed the area to forest in the early 20th century, it was left standing and absorbed into a row of American oaks planted as a windbreak/plot boundary. DISTANCE CAVEAT: Bladel/Ten Vorsel is about 16 km from Hilvarenbeek's own tree (hvb_001, the Gebodenlinde); this is a separate day-trip stop by car, not a joint walk, and the page should say so plainly.
